name: Executive Function and Behavior Support
title: Executive Function and Behavior Support
answer: Executive function and behavior support uses AI to help students with disabilities plan and organize their work, to create visual schedules and social narratives, and to chart behavior data so patterns can be seen. It matters because these supports address real barriers to learning while keeping the student's own skill building as the goal. The decisions about what a pattern means and what to change stay with the people who know the student.

sections.body: Many students with disabilities find executive function difficult, which covers planning, organizing and managing time. AI can take a large assignment and break it into smaller steps with deadlines attached. A student can then place those steps on a calendar, and students aged 13 and older can use a school account for planning help. The aim is not to make the student reliant on the tool but to build the student's own skills over time. Visual schedules and social narratives serve a related purpose by showing students with autism or anxiety what to expect, and behavior plans rest on recorded data about what happens before and after a behavior.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In the classroom, a student can use a calendar to lay out the steps of a big assignment, and older students, from age 13, can use a school account for planning support. Teachers and counselors create visual schedules and social narratives with tools such as Boardmaker and Canva for Education, and the special education teacher or counselor reviews any narrative written for a particular student so it stays simple, positive and true to that student's situation. For behavior, staff record when behaviors occur, what came before and what followed, and spreadsheet features can chart that data and point to patterns such as behaviors clustering at certain times or in certain settings. The behavior team then reads those patterns and decides what to change.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure or finding for this idea, so it rests on practice rather than research. What it offers instead is guidance drawn from school experience, including the aim of building the student's own skills rather than dependence on the tool, and the requirement that narratives be reviewed by the special education teacher or counselor and kept simple, positive and true to the student.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: A chart cannot know why a student is struggling, so the behavior team, not the tool, interprets the patterns and decides what to change. Social narratives must be reviewed by the special education teacher or counselor and must be simple, positive and true to the student's situation. Planning help through a school account is limited to students 13 and older. The larger limit is dependence: the purpose of breaking assignments into steps is to build the student's own executive function over time, not to leave the student reliant on the tool.
